summary: Learners aged 11–13 learn to diagnose three distinct kinds of dietary imbalance — obesity as a sustained energy surplus, starvation as a severe energy deficit, and deficiency disease as the lack of a specific nutrient — and to reason from a symptom or scenario back to its specific dietary cause, naming the missing nutrient. The core skill is diagnostic cause–effect, not just reciting definitions. Activities centre on examining cases and 'fixing' diets so that the key insight can emerge: feeding more total food does not cure a deficiency disease; only the specific missing nutrient does.
misconceptions: Thinking deficiency disease just means 'not eating enough food', rather than missing one specific nutrient.
Believing eating more of anything cures a deficiency (only the missing nutrient does).
Assuming obesity is simply 'eating too much' without the energy-surplus framing, or moralising it.
Thinking dietary damage is always quickly reversible.
Confusing which nutrient causes which disease (e.g. mixing up scurvy and rickets).

activities.title: Diet clinic: diagnose the cause and fix the diet
steps: Examine a patient who presents with a sign, e.g. bleeding gums and loosening teeth, bowed/soft legs, persistent tiredness, steady weight gain, or severe wasting.
Read the patient's diet log and form an explicit hypothesis: too much energy overall, too little energy overall, or a specific missing nutrient — and if a deficiency, name which nutrient.

Edit the diet to test the hypothesis (for example, first try simply adding more of the same foods already in the log, then try adding a specific nutrient such as vitamin C), and observe whether the patient's condition improves (some effects, such as bone deformity from rickets, may only partly reverse).
State in your own words why your chosen change worked or failed — tie the outcome to surplus, deficit, or a specific missing nutrient.
Work through at least two deficiency cases (e.g. scurvy/vitamin C and rickets/vitamin D with calcium) plus one surplus and one deficit case so all three failure modes are practised.
activities.insight: A deficiency disease is caused by the lack of a specific nutrient (or closely linked nutrients, such as vitamin D and calcium in rickets), not by eating too little food overall; you can eat plenty of energy-rich food and still be ill. This is distinct from starvation (too little energy) and obesity (too much energy).

activities.title: Body-map of deficiency signs (naming layer)
steps: Explore a body-map illustration with tappable signs: select bleeding gums to reveal 'scurvy — too little vitamin C'; select bowed/soft legs to reveal 'rickets — too little vitamin D/calcium'; add a sign for iron deficiency (anaemia — persistent tiredness/pallor).

Open a lift-the-flap prompt: 'Is a deficiency disease caused by eating too little food?' → 'No — by missing a specific nutrient (for rickets, vitamin D and/or calcium), which can happen even on plenty of food.'
Build or complete a disease → missing-nutrient table from the signs you uncover (scurvy/vitamin C, rickets/vitamin D with calcium, anaemia/iron).
activities.insight: Each deficiency disease pairs with a specific missing nutrient and a recognisable sign, so a symptom can be read back to its cause.

activities.title: Classify and match: surplus, deficit, or specific deficiency
steps: Match each deficiency disease to its missing nutrient (scurvy→vitamin C; rickets→vitamin D/calcium; anaemia→iron).
Categorise short scenarios as energy surplus, energy deficit, or specific-nutrient deficiency.
Answer a short-response item explaining why the harm from a poor diet can be long-term or sometimes irreversible (e.g. rickets affecting bone development).
activities.insight: The three failure modes are distinct categories, and poor-diet harm can accumulate over time rather than appearing immediately.

activities.title: Historical case: the scurvy voyage (narrative option)
steps: Talk through a scenario with a ship's surgeon or dietitian investigating why well-fed sailors fall ill on a long voyage (bread and salted meat, no fresh fruit or vegetables).
Propose what single nutrient is missing and where it would come from, and respond to follow-up questions that test whether 'plenty of food' explains the illness.
Explain how this case differs from starvation.
activities.insight: A diet can be sufficient in quantity yet still be missing a specific nutrient, so eating plenty of food does not guarantee a balanced diet.

checkQuestion: A sailor on a long voyage eats plenty of food every day — lots of bread and salted meat — so he certainly isn't starving. Yet his gums bleed, his teeth loosen and old wounds reopen: he has scurvy. How can someone eating plenty of food still get a disease like this? Explain.
checkAnswer: Because a deficiency disease isn't about the AMOUNT of food but about a specific missing nutrient — scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C, found in fresh fruit and vegetables, which the sailor's diet lacked. You can eat plenty of energy-rich food and still be ill if your diet is missing a particular vitamin or mineral. A diet must be balanced, not just sufficient in quantity.
